Match variables to a group template

gly_pattern_hunter.Rd

Assign each sample the template score for its experimental group and correlate each variable's abundance with those scores. Positive and negative coefficients identify matches in opposite directions.

Usage

gly_pattern_hunter(
  exp,
  template,
  group_col = "group",
  method = "pearson",
  p_adj_method = "BH",
  add_info = TRUE,
  log_transform = NULL
)

Arguments

exp

A glyexp::GlycomicSE() or glyexp::GlycoproteomicSE() object, or another SummarizedExperiment containing an expression matrix and sample information.

template

A named numeric vector with one finite score for each observed group in group_col. Names must match the group labels exactly. Groups may share a score. At least two distinct scores are required.

group_col

Name of the sample metadata column containing the group labels. Each sample must have a non-missing, non-empty label.

method

Correlation coefficient, one of "pearson" (default), "spearman", or "kendall".

p_adj_method

A character string specifying the method to adjust p-values. See p.adjust.methods for available methods. Default is "BH". If NULL, no adjustment is performed.

add_info

Whether to include variable annotations in the tidy result.

log_transform

NULL (default) uses metadata(exp)$scale to avoid logging data twice. TRUE requests the method's log transformation for raw data; if the input is already on "log", "log2", "log10", or "logx", it warns and uses the supplied values unchanged. FALSE always uses the supplied values unchanged. This argument must be named when it follows ....

Value

A glystats_pattern_hunter_res object inheriting from glystats_res. get_tidy_result() returns one row per input variable in assay order.

  • .variable gives the SE variable ID (variable for legacy inputs).

  • cor is the signed correlation coefficient.

  • n_samples, n_groups, and n_scores count the finite samples, represented groups, and distinct template scores for the variable.

  • p_val is the two-sided p-value and p_adj is its adjusted value. Setting p_adj_method = NULL omits p_adj.

get_raw_result() returns a list of stats::cor.test() results named by variable ID, with NULL for untestable variables. The result records template, group_col, method, p_adj_method, the input meta_data, and the preprocessing used. SE inputs also retain the identifiers mapping described in gly_identity.

Details

Each finite sample observation contributes once. Groups with more observed samples have more weight. For each variable, the test uses the groups and scores represented among its finite abundances on the analysis scale. If a group is entirely missing, the coefficient describes the remaining groups. A test requires at least three such samples, two distinct template scores, and variation in abundance. Other rows retain their counts and receive NA for the coefficient and p-values.

Raw abundances use log2(x + 1e-6) by default. See gly_scale for scale overrides. With relative abundances, a match describes changes only relative to the normalization reference, such as the total measured abundance. Even a strong positive correlation with an increasing template can include a decrease between adjacent groups.

The two-sided tests assume independent samples and a prespecified template. For fixed scores, the Pearson test is the slope test in a linear regression with independent normal errors of constant variance. The rank tests assume exchangeability under independence. Spearman uses average ranks for ties and Kendall uses tau-b. With ties, stats::cor.test() uses approximate rank-test p-values, which can be inaccurate with few samples. Without ties, it uses its usual sample-size-dependent calculation.

Multiplicity adjustment covers the testable variables for this template. If several templates are screened, account for the full set of tests. A template chosen after inspecting the data needs independent validation.

References

Pavlidis P, Noble WS (2001). Analysis of strain and regional variation in gene expression in mouse brain. Genome Biology, 2, research0042. doi:10.1186/gb-2001-2-10-research0042 .

Pavlidis P (2003). Using ANOVA for gene selection from microarray studies of the nervous system. Methods, 31, 282-289. doi:10.1016/S1046-2023(03)00157-9 .

For a related pattern search in metabolomics, see Xia J, Mandal R, Sinelnikov IV, Broadhurst D, Wishart DS (2012). MetaboAnalyst 2.0—a comprehensive server for metabolomic data analysis. Nucleic Acids Research, 40, W127-W133. doi:10.1093/nar/gks374 .

Examples

exp <- glyexp::real_experiment2
groups <- SummarizedExperiment::colData(exp)$group
exp <- exp[1:5, groups %in% c("H", "C")]
res <- gly_pattern_hunter(exp, template = c(H = 0, C = 1), add_info = FALSE)
get_tidy_result(res)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 7
#>   .variable                     cor n_samples n_groups n_scores p_val p_adj

#> 3 Hex(5)HexNAc(2)          0.153           73        2        2 0.196 0.982
#> 4 Hex(6)HexNAc(4)NeuAc(2)  0.000808        69        2        2 0.995 0.995
#> 5 Hex(4)HexNAc(3)         -0.0261          72        2        2 0.828 0.995
